Finally, we prove that $(R_H(A),K_{\mathrm{ref}}(A))$ is factorizable if and only if $(H,R)$ is factorizable and $A$ is simple as an algebra.

papers.title: What crossing symmetry forbids just above $c=1$
papers.abstract: What does a unitary two-dimensional conformal field theory look like just above $c=1$? Using the numerical conformal bootstrap, we study the four-point function of a scalar Virasoro primary $ϕ$ such that no primary lighter than $ϕ$ appears in its operator product expansion with itself. Slightly above $c=1$, crossing symmetry excludes the interval $0.17\lesssimΔ_ϕ\lesssim1$, although the compact boson realizes every such $Δ_ϕ$ at $c=1$. Combining this exclusion with results from the modular bootstrap, we show that the lightest primary of a compact unitary conformal field theory at $c=1.0005$ or $1.001$ has dimension $Δ_{\rm gap}<0.17$. Further from $c=1$, the largest excluded central charge at fixed $Δ_ϕ$ has two sharp minima near $Δ_ϕ=1/2$ and $4/7$. At these values it lies within $2\times10^{-7}$ of $c=8/7$, where the $\mathbb{Z}_5$ parafermion and its charge-conjugation orbifold have scalars of exactly these dimensions.

papers.title: Hodge--Riemann relations for $m$-positive and generalized $m$-positive forms
papers.abstract: We study strong positivity and Hodge--Riemann relations for real $(1,1)$-forms satisfying generalized $m$-positivity conditions. Every good prefix, defined via the hyperbolicity cones of successive directional derivatives of the determinant, has a strictly strongly positive product and satisfies the Hodge--Riemann relations in all bidegrees. Allowing boundary factors, we prove that the hyperbolicity cone of every nonzero product of an almost-good prefix coincides with the polarizing component of its exterior-algebra quotient. As a special case, we obtain the full mixed Hodge--Riemann relations for ordinary $m$-positive forms without assuming semipositivity. We also establish the Hodge--Riemann relations for weakly $(m,l)$-positive forms in all bidegrees $(p,q)$ with $p+q\le m$ and $\max\{p,q\}\ge l$. For $l=1$ and $m\ge2$, we deduce that the associated $(m-1)$-th power map is a real-analytic diffeomorphism onto the cone of strictly positive $(d-1,d-1)$-forms. Adapting the $L^2$ method of Dinh and Nguyên, we pass from these pointwise results to the cohomology of compact Kähler manifolds. Finally, we study numerical criteria, generalized complex Hessian equations, and sharp reverse Khovanskii--Teissier inequalities in the sequential setting.

papers.title: Generalized Wishart processes under nonlinear expectation
papers.abstract: We develop a theory of generalized Wishart processes within the framework of $G$-expectation, with $G$-Dyson Brownian motion and the $G$-Wishart process as two typical examples. In contrast to the classical setting, we show that $G$-Dyson Brownian motion may exhibit collisions and provide a sufficient condition ensuring the non-collision property of the eigenvalues of generalized Wishart processes. We then derive the equations governing the high-dimensional limits of the empirical spectral measures under $G$-expectation, leading to the corresponding semicircle law for $G$-Dyson Brownian motion and Marchenko--Pastur law for the $G$-Wishart process.

papers.title: Write Facts the Way Models Read Them: Lifting the Two-Hop Curse
papers.abstract: A language model that learns a new fact by fine-tuning can repeat it but cannot reason with it: taught that a person is a citizen of a new country, it still cannot say, without chain-of-thought, who the head of state of that person's country is. This two-hop curse is widely treated as a reasoning deficit, and the strongest knowledge editors answer it with synthesized reasoning data. We show that the reasoning is intact and the writing is wrong. Fine-tuning writes a new fact as an answer to be said, whereas the second hop reads the bridge ("that person's country") as an entity, from the middle layers on: patching the model's own representation of the entity into the bridge at those layers largely restores the second hop, yet after fine-tuning the bridge there is no closer to the new entity than before the edit. We therefore propose read-equivalent writing (Legible): one loss term makes the bridge phrase, at the layer where the second hop finishes reading it, match the model's own reading of the new entity, and keeps the same relation's other subjects unchanged. Phrases and targets come from the edited model itself, and no multi-hop training data is used. Across Qwen2.5, Llama-3 and Qwen3, Legible (I) composes learned facts more often than the model composes its own knowledge, on MQuAKE's two-hop-curse questions; (II) reaches 1.8-2.6x the bridge accuracy of CaKE, whose reasoning data composes no better than plain fine-tuning, and has the best average over composition, accuracy and locality against four families of writers; and (III) lifts the curse on RippleEdits, on the benchmark of Balesni et al., who named the curse, and at 14B.

papers.title: Lightweight Representation Learning for Low Tucker Rank Tensors
papers.abstract: Iterative estimators for low Tucker rank tensors, such as HOOI, nuclear-norm proximal and ADMM methods, Frank-Wolfe and scaled gradient descent, form large objects in every iteration: unfoldings, Kronecker operators, full SVDs and ambient iterates. The update uses little of these objects, yet they make memory the limiting resource on large tensors and on edge-sized devices. Remedies for each of these costs are known. However, it is unclear when a rewriting keeps the iterates unchanged, and where it pays off against efficient implementations. We therefore present a trajectory-preserving lightweight evaluation. First, we state exactness as an intertwining relation between the stored state and the reference iteration. Second, we show that three known components satisfy this relation for five estimators: computing only the singular triplets that an update needs, contracting without Kronecker products, and storing sparse-plus-factored states. As a result, the iterates and all guarantees of the reference estimator stay the same. On an A100 GPU, with the input data counted in the memory, lightweight HOOI needs the least memory of 15 HOOI-type methods at every size ($95\times$ less beyond the input than the lightest exact implementation on $800^3$ tensors), and it is the fastest method that reaches the HOOI estimate on the largest tensors. Against efficient public code, ours is faster and lighter for three of five estimators. On a surveillance video and a satellite hyperspectral cube, ours is the only implementation that fits a 1 GiB and a 4 GiB device. Finally, we show that the memory and time gains need separate conditions, and we identify where these conditions fail.

papers.title: Intervenable Concept Dynamics for Video Activity Forecasting
papers.abstract: Concept bottleneck models route predictions through human-understandable concepts, making their intermediate states inspectable and editable. Extending this model family to forecasting requires modeling how concept activations evolve over time as objects, actions, and their interactions change, yet existing CBMs ground concepts only in observed inputs and do not forecast their future evolution. We study this problem using videos of ongoing activities and forecast future activities through a named-concept state. We propose TRACE-CBM (Temporal Relational Activity Concept Evolution), which first refines observed concept activations with sparse spatio-temporal graphs. It then recursively predicts future concept states, conditioning each transition on the prior activity distribution, and decodes both observed and predicted states with a shared activity classifier. At inference time, the model supports editing concept values, activity activations, and learned edges without parameter updates, exposing the relational spatio-temporal dependencies used for forecasting. Across multiple datasets, TRACE improves observed-activity accuracy over concept-based methods and stays close to matched black-box forecasters in forecast accuracy. Intervention experiments show that concept edits correct part of the initially incorrect forecasts without flipping initially correct ones, and that activity-belief edits can steer forecasts toward a requested activity. Code: https://github.com/patrick-knab/TRACE-CBM

papers.title: Splitting Compositions of Monotone Operators
papers.abstract: Coupled convex optimisation equilibria and nonlinear circuits lead to inclusions of the form $0 \in Hx + A(Bx) - b$, where $A$ and $B$ are maximally monotone but the complete operator need not be monotone. We develop a one-parameter family of triangular warped-resolvent algorithms on product Hilbert spaces to solve such inclusions. Introducing $y \in Bx$ exposes a directed lift, and a composition-adapted kernel organizes each iteration into one evaluation of $H$ and one ordinary resolvent evaluation per factor block. A nonnegative multi-block gain matrix certifies a unique lifted solution, global linear convergence, and residual error bounds. An exact Schur reduction converts the $2n \times 2n$ condition into an equivalent $n \times n$ criterion. For nonpositive extrapolation, this criterion is necessary and sufficient to guarantee a unique fixed point and global linear convergence for all problems satisfying the given gain bounds. Minimum-gain estimates characterize its exact finite-stepsize feasibility boundary. A negative-coupling rotation family exhibits certified convergence when neither the original operator nor its specified lift admits a fixed positive-definite monotonicity metric. For a nonlinear periodic RLC circuit, we establish continuous-time nonmonotonicity and derive a computable convergence certificate. Our algorithm is demonstrated on a periodic circuit simulation problem.

papers.title: On the median of the beta distribution in relation to the median of the gamma distribution
papers.abstract: The median of the beta distribution has no closed form, but it is closely tied to the median of the gamma distribution. Kerman's approximation has the ratio form $g(α)/(g(α)+g(β))$ with $g(x) = x - 1/3$, a lower bound on the gamma median, and it is a lower bound on the beta median for $1/3 < α< β$. The ratio form built from the true gamma median is a tighter lower bound, asymptotically exact as $β\to \infty$. The ratio form built from the Wilson-Hilferty approximation to the gamma median, implicit in a classical approximation to the $F$ distribution but little known as an approximation to the beta median, is an upper bound on the line $α= 1$ and, along each ray $β= rα$ with $r > 1$, for large shape parameters. The ratio form that is exact on the lines $α= 1$ and $β= 1$, $(2^{1/β} - 1)/(2^{1/α} + 2^{1/β} - 2)$, is numerically within 0.3% of the median when both shape parameters are at least 1, and provably less than 25% above it for $α\le β$; it yields a new approximation to the gamma median, which is an upper bound on it for shape parameter below 1 and a lower bound above 1. Interpolating between it and a ratio form with a $1/x$ correction gives, with no fitted constant, an approximation within 0.016% of the median when both shape parameters are at least 1. No ratio form gives the beta median exactly. For large shape parameters, the logit of the median has an explicit second-order expansion. For small shape parameters, bounds in elementary functions are asymptotically tight. An approximation in elementary functions that joins the two ends, with four fitted constants, is exact on the lines $α= 1$, $β= 1$, and $α= β$, and numerically within 0.065% of the median over the whole domain. Most of the proofs are machine-verified in Lean 4.

papers.title: Atom as an Agent: Emergent Order by Collective Predictive Coding
papers.abstract: What is the intrinsic reason of emergence of macroscopic order parameter out of microscopic systems? In this article, we apply to physics the collective predictive coding (CPC), the theory of language/symbol emergence. As our language emerges out of our human communications, physical macroscopic order parameter emerges out of communications among atoms --- each atom is regarded as an agent who predicts each other's behavior through inference. We present three examples of classical spin systems: two-dimensional ferromagnetic and antiferromagnetic Ising models, a two-dimensional spin model with competing stripe orders, and the fully connected Sherrington--Kirkpatrick spin-glass model. In all of these examples, proper macroscopic order parameters including the replica overlap emerge automatically through communication informatics of CPC, only from observed spin configurations. We call the learned macroscopic coordinate the collective predictive order. Furthermore, for the ferromagnetic and antiferromagnetic Ising models, the equilibrium distribution of the collective predictive order yields an emergent potential with the symmetry and thermal evolution characteristic of a Landau potential. Notably, the emergence of the collective predictive order does not refer to any structure of microscopic Hamiltonians/Lagrangians. Thus our ``Atom-as-an-Agent" (AaaA) principle offers a completely data-driven method for the emergence of macroscopic order, that is, machine learning physics.

papers.title: LabWorld: Learning Interactive 4D Worlds for Scientific Experimentation
papers.abstract: Autonomous scientific agents must not only reason about experiments but also interact with the physical environments in which they are executed. Existing laboratory simulators typically rely on manually constructed assets and predefined procedures, while laboratory videos capture real equipment, layouts, and interactions but leave this information implicit in pixels. We introduce LabWorld, an agent-driven Real2Sim framework for reconstructing interactive 4D laboratory worlds from monocular RGB video. LabWorld recovers reusable 3D assets, a metric scene, time-varying object states, and procedure events. Multi-frame observations provide complementary evidence for asset and scene reconstruction, while motion reconstruction combines visual and geometric observations with event constraints encoding the spatial and temporal requirements of laboratory interactions. We evaluate LabWorld on real pipetting and vortexing videos collected in our laboratory against general-purpose agentic and dedicated reconstruction baselines. For pipetting, LabWorld achieves a mean Mask IoU of 0.501, exceeding the strongest baseline by 0.033. For vortexing, it achieves a mean Tube-Length-Normalized PCK-AUC of 0.638, exceeding the strongest baseline by 0.035. On five pipetting videos, event-conditioned reconstruction increases the fraction of modeled physical constraints satisfied from 14.3% (5/35) to 100% (35/35). The resulting worlds expose geometry, motion, articulation, and events as explicit, editable state for replay, inspection, and future embodied scientific systems.

papers.title: Effective Chebotarev-Sato-Tate distribution for Abelian varieties with applications
papers.abstract: In this paper, we aim to establish a uniform effective form of the Chebotarev-Sato-Tate distribution for abelian varieties with a connected Sato-Tate group, conditional on standard analytic conjectures for L-functions attached to the relevant irreducible representations. This improves on the exponent of Bucur, Fite, and Kedlaya (Theorem 1.1, 2024) whenever the Sato-Tate group has rank greater than one. We also establish a variant for prime-dependent regions of the Sato-Tate group and finite Galois extensions that vary with the counting parameter. As an application, for a normalized non-CM newform f of weight 2 and level N with a quadratic coefficient field, we obtain a conditional upper bound for Pi(x):=|{p<= x: p does not divide N, a(p) is in Q}|, where a(p) is the pth Fourier coefficient of f. In addition, we formulate a discrepancy conjecture that allows us to prove Murty's asymptotic prediction (Conjecture 3.4, 1999) for Pi(x).

papers.title: Ranking Function Generation with LLMs for Termination
papers.abstract: Ranking functions are a fundamental technique for proving loop termination, but synthesizing them remains challenging and often requires substantial expertise. Despite considerable progress in their automated synthesis, existing approaches remain limited in their effectiveness. We propose RAINFALL, a neuro-symbolic framework that tightly integrates large language models (LLMs) with symbolic verification. To our best knowledge, RAINFALL is the first to employ a generate-verify-refine paradigm for LLM-based ranking function synthesis. RAINFALL formulates ranking function synthesis as a constrained code-completion task, inserting placeholders into the input program that the LLM must fill in four predefined slots per loop. The resulting program is checked by a symbolic verifier. Successful verification yields a valid ranking function, while verification failures produce diagnostics that are translated into natural-language feedback to guide iterative refinement. We evaluate RAINFALL on two public benchmark suites comprising 358 terminating C programs. Using DeepSeek-V4.1-Flash, RAINFALL synthesizes verified ranking functions for 333 programs (93.02%), outperforming all evaluated baselines. Notably, it solves 22 more programs than PROTON 2.1, the winner of the SV-COMP 2026 Termination Category. Combining RAINFALL with PROTON 2.1 further increases the success rate to 96.65% (346/358 programs). Ablation studies demonstrate the contributions of placeholder contracts, few-shot examples, symbolic verification, and diagnostic feedback, while experiments across different LLMs establish the broader applicability of the framework.

papers.title: The Choice Number of Random Graphs
papers.abstract: In 1999, Alon, Krivelevich and Sudakov conjectured that the choice number and chromatic number of the random graph $G(n,p)$ are asymptotically equal whenever $np\to\infty$. We prove their conjecture, showing that, with high probability, $$\mathrm{ch}(G(n,p))=(1+o(1))χ(G(n,p))$$ whenever $np\to\infty$. This improves the bound $\mathrm{ch}(G(n,p))\le(2+o(1))χ(G(n,p))$ for $np\to\infty$ and $p\le0.9$ obtained by Krivelevich and Vu in 2001. Our proof distinguishes two cases according to the size of independent sets. When independent sets of growing size are available, we establish a sharper uniform independent-set estimate that eliminates the factor-two loss in the bound of Krivelevich and Vu. When independent sets have bounded size, we establish a deterministic result showing that, under a suitable uniform independent-set condition, a proper colouring with bounded colour-class sizes yields an asymptotically matching upper bound on the choice number.

papers.title: Diagnosing and Mitigating Long-Session Degradation in Full-Duplex Speech Models
papers.abstract: End-to-end full-duplex spoken dialogue models enable natural, real-time spoken interactions with interruptions, backchannels, and overlapping speech. Prior evaluations have assessed diverse interaction capabilities and identified some degradation patterns across conversational turns. However, how model behavior evolves over extended sessions remains insufficiently understood. In this work, we address this gap by systematically characterizing long-session degradation and developing efficient methods to mitigate it. We introduce a closed-loop evaluation framework for long-session stability and apply it to several publicly available full-duplex speech models, revealing degradation over time in responsiveness, spoken content quality, and voice consistency. To mitigate this degradation, we propose a self-distillation-based training framework for lightweight LoRA adaptation that improves long-session stability with a small amount of additional training. We further introduce a two-resolution context (TRC) architecture that preserves recent interactions in full detail while compressing older interaction history into key-value representations. We evaluate our methods on three models with distinct architectures, assessing long-session stability, information retention, and computational efficiency. Across all three models, we show that LoRA adaptation mitigates performance degradation over ten-minute sessions, while adding TRC extends these gains beyond the training session length and reduces KV-cache growth by more than 90%.

papers.title: Deletion Is Not Substitution: Component Attribution in a Layered Prompt-Injection Gateway for LLM Tool Calls
papers.abstract: Prompt-injection defenses for LLM agents are commonly built as cascades of increasingly costly stages, and ablation studies evaluate their components by switching each stage off and counting the detections lost. In a cascade, however, stages are not independent: a stage's contribution depends on what is routed to it and how its verdicts are enforced, so deletion-based ablation can mislead. We test this on BARBICAN, a four-tier, fail-closed gateway for Model Context Protocol tool calls, developed in our group, that routes borderline inputs to a neural arbitrator. After reproducing its recorded evaluation exactly, we apply deletion, constant substitution, repair and transplant to its arbitration stage. The findings rest on over thirty instrumented runs over 25,000 prompts, two platforms, an independent check set and six versions from the system's history. Depending on how "switching off" is defined, deletion credits the stage with contributions that differ by more than an order of magnitude, whereas substitution shows that its verdicts can affect only a few inputs, all attacks. Neither repairing the stage nor replacing it with a much stronger classifier changed the system appreciably: its influence is set by its position, not its quality. An observation that bounds the decisions a routed stage can change explains this, and a cascade of public classifiers reproduces it whenever routing concentrates attacks. Treating constant verdicts as mutants, we derive a continuous-integration gate that detects a stage whose verdicts cannot reach the output and, in light of these results, offer a three-point roadmap for ablation studies.

papers.title: Superlinear Convergence of Cyclic Gradient Methods with Historical Ritz Step Sizes
papers.abstract: The long-step Barzilai-Borwein (BB1) method, cyclic BB1, and limited memory steepest descent (LMSD) are special cases of limited memory steepest descent with retards (LMSDR), a family of methods using historical Ritz step sizes. We analyze a cyclic Ritz-step rule within LMSDR and a sampled LMSDR variant on strictly convex quadratics, seeking R-superlinear convergence guarantees in higher spectral dimensions. Let $n$ be the problem dimension and $m$ the history length. In exact arithmetic, we begin at $n=m+1$, the first dimension beyond the finite-termination case, and obtain an exact doubly exponential rate per gradient update for rolling reuse outside an explicit, possibly empty exceptional set. We extend this rate to nonempty open sets for $m+1<n\le2m$ when each Ritz step is reused $\ell\ge4$ times. To go beyond this range, we rebuild the history with $m$ sampling updates at each cycle. With positive sampling steps $τ$ chosen in advance and factors $1-τλ_i$ uniformly bounded in modulus and away from zero, this gives almost-everywhere doubly exponential convergence when $(2\ell-1)^m>\binom{n-1}{m}$. For any $n>m$, increasing $\ell$ eventually satisfies this condition. Geometrically spaced choices among finitely many sampling lists preserve the guarantee.

papers.title: DeepAVR: Deep Analysis via Multi-Agent Collaboration for Automated Vulnerability Repair
papers.abstract: Automated Vulnerability Repair (AVR) has emerged as a promising approach to identifying and fixing software vulnerabilities autonomously. Early LLM-based approaches focused on patch generation under the assumption of perfect fault localization, while recent end-to-end methods attempt to repair vulnerabilities directly from sanitizer logs. However, these methods often fail when the root cause is deeply hidden, either physically distant from the crash site or logically masked by interdependent errors, making the initial report insufficient. We propose DeepAVR, a multi-agent framework that transforms intermediate repair outcomes into structured diagnostic feedback. It coordinates specialized agents for fault localization, patch generation, compilation, security and functionality validation, and patch review to iteratively refine localization and patch hypotheses. Specifically, DeepAVR introduces patch-conditioned re-localization, using execution results from intermediate patches to uncover hidden root causes, and root-cause-oriented patch review to identify symptom-level fixes and incomplete repairs that escape execution-based validation. Evaluation on VulnLoc, a real-world C/C++ vulnerability repair dataset, shows that DeepAVR outperforms prior methods, generating correct patches for 92.3% of vulnerabilities. Evaluation on SAN2VULN demonstrates its ability to repair vulnerabilities unseen during training. On SEC-bench, DeepAVR outperforms the evaluated baselines on cases whose fixes lie outside the crash-site function.

papers.title: The Delayed Countdown Method for Validating Review-Oriented AI Workflows in eDiscovery
papers.abstract: Review-oriented workflows have become the dominant approach to AI-assisted document review in electronic discovery (eDiscovery). How to validate the effectiveness of review-oriented workflows has, however, remained a confusing and controversial topic in technology-assisted review (TAR) in the law. We examine the sources of this controversy, and propose a simple and practical evaluation approach for review-oriented workflows. Our Delayed Countdown method is easily incorporated into existing review-oriented workflows and software, is compatible with arbitrary stopping rules, and produces valid frequentist confidence intervals on effectiveness. We explain the conceptual foundations of the method, provide example computations, discuss the handling of logically impossible recall values, and suggest future work on decreasing review costs. (This paper was submitted October 1, 2026 to The Tenth Annual Workshop on Applications of Artificial Intelligence in the Legal Industry.)

papers.title: Analysis of a coronal hole jet in the chromosphere and the transition region with IRIS data and SDO observations
papers.abstract: Coronal jets are transient phenomena that occur throughout the solar atmosphere, often triggered by the activation of mini-filaments. Jets are an important field of study, as they are believed to contribute to the mass supply of the solar wind. We study a small-scale solar jet occurring in a low-latitude coronal hole, focusing on traces of the jet eruption to the lower atmosphere, utilizing chromospheric and transition region diagnostics. We also investigate the possible mechanisms and dynamic conditions leading to its onset. We analyze ultraviolet spectra from the Interface Region Imaging Spectrograph to investigate chromospheric dynamics and their connection to the transition region, using diagnostics of the Mg II k 2796.35 Å and Si IV 1393.75 Å lines, together with non-LTE inversions. We complement this analysis with multiwavelength imaging and magnetograms from the Solar Dynamics Observatory, as well as magnetic field modeling. The analysis of Mg II k and Si IV parameters reveals a coupling between chromospheric and transition region plasma dynamics. Profiles on the jet spire present deeper central reversals, larger peak separations and higher transition region Doppler velocities. The jet initiation is associated with a mini-filament-like structure, preceded by dynamic variations in the photospheric magnetic field. We find single-peaked Mg II k profiles at one of its footpoints, possibly indicating plasma drainage. The presence of a null point and a quasi-separatrix layer suggests that reconnection can play a role in the mini-filament-like structure destabilization and jet eruption. This study suggests that the signature and possibly the origin of coronal jets can be traced down to the chromosphere. The detailed analysis of the Mg II k profiles at the jet spire and the mini-filament-like structure may provide valuable observational constraints for future MHD simulations.

papers.title: One Evaluation Is Enough: Inversion-Free Image Editing with Trajectory Correction
papers.abstract: Real-image editing commonly relies on inversion and iterative sampling, while efficient one-step editors often stabilize a large update by estimating and averaging editing fields at multiple noise levels. We ask a stricter question: is a single temporal field evaluation sufficient for reliable inversion-free editing? Our answer rests on a previously underused duality in a variance-preserving (VP) one-step model: one source-target query at a shared noisy state simultaneously determines a local angular semantic tangent and a clean endpoint displacement. We integrate the tangent over the analytically known remaining VP angle to obtain a nominal one-step transport, and use the endpoint displacement to correct its long-horizon extrapolation through a constrained projection. This transport-first, correction-second construction yields Endpoint-Calibrated Transport (ECT), a closed-form, training-free editor requiring only one noise level, two text conditions packed into one denoiser batch, and one latent update. ECT requires no image inversion, trajectory integration, second temporal observation, or iterative optimization, and can be directly applied to pretrained epsilon-prediction VP one-step generators. Across the reported benchmark settings, ECT delivers stable gains in editing quality within an extremely short editing time.

papers.title: CoRE: Relating Fine-Grained Chest X-ray Findings in Anatomical Context
papers.abstract: Chest X-ray interpretation depends on both the anatomical location of findings and their relationships with other abnormalities. However, relations defined over global finding labels do not explicitly distinguish the same finding across anatomical locations. We propose CoRE(Co-occurrence-guided Region Evidence), a framework that incorporates relationships among findings and anatomical context into fine-grained chest X-ray prediction. It groups anatomical region-finding labels by co-occurrence and uses these groups to guide shared representation learning through visual prompt tuning on a frozen vision transformer. The predictions are supplemented by an anatomically supervised region-evidence stream through region-matched logit residuals. Experiments on MIMIC-CXR with Chest ImaGenome annotations show that CoRE improves region-finding classification over standard and relation-aware prompt-based baselines. Quantitative evaluations on MS-CXR and the Chest ImaGenome gold standard show improved finding localization, supported by qualitative comparisons. CoRE also improves finding-level classification on mapped finding labels in external VinDr-CXR and CheXpert datasets without target-domain adaptation. These results demonstrate the value of jointly modeling finding relationships and anatomical context for fine-grained chest X-ray analysis.

papers.title: How Do DiTs Denoise? An Aggregator-Predictor View of Attention and MLPs
papers.abstract: Local denoising helps explain diffusion generalization. How do diffusion transformers (DiTs) implement it? Our aggregator--predictor framework decomposes population local denoising into context aggregation and patch prediction. Single-layer algebra motivates treating attention and MLP as estimators of these quantities. We test this view on pixel DiTs and pretrained U-ViT, JiT, and latent flow models across datasets and resolutions from $64\times64$ to $256\times256$. We find that (1) attention-selected context transfers across models, and adapting the selected context to each noisy image improves denoising at low noise; (2) DiTs can share a single learned key--value bank across layers for patch prediction while retaining generation quality comparable to DiTs with a separate MLP in each layer; and (3) across related face domains, transplanting jointly adapted QK preserves more source-associated appearance, while transplanting adapted VO+MLP produces more target-associated appearance. Motivated by these findings, we test matched-budget fine-tuning on MetFaces. Across three backbones, adapting VO, MLP, or both with QK frozen yields competitive generation quality, while adapting QK alone performs worse. These results illustrate how DiT components can be reused, replaced, and adapted.

papers.title: ReTRACE: Feedback-Guided LLM Agent in a Chemistry Harness for Retrosynthesis Planning
papers.abstract: Computer-aided retrosynthesis has progressed through single-step prediction, tree search and route scoring, yet complex targets still require route-level judgement where stereochemistry, functional-group compatibility, cost and greenness interact. Here we present \textbf{\mbox{ReTRACE}} (\textbf{RE}trosynthesis with \textbf{T}ool-orchestrated \textbf{R}easoning \textbf{A}nd \textbf{C}ontext-aware \textbf{E}vidence), an agent that places a large language model (LLM) inside a deterministic chemistry harness integrating molecular tools, heterogeneous single-step prediction engines, purchasable building-block libraries, an external route memory and a multi-criterion evaluator. To assess chemical validity beyond stock termination, we introduce Audit@k, a two-stage metric combining programmatic structural checks with adversarial LLM review that closely tracks expert judgement. ReTRACE learns from harness feedback on two timescales: within a run, it diagnoses weak sub-scores and backtracks to revise disconnections; across runs, trajectories and audit verdicts are distilled through a three-stage post-training pipeline into an open-weight coordinator, ReTRACE-27B, which completes routes for all 40 evaluation targets and raises Audit@1 from 11/40 (27.5\%) to 23/40 (57.5\%). Across Retro*-190, JMC2025 and FDA30, ReTRACE with GPT-6.2 Astra achieves Audit@1 of 97.9\%, 99.3\% and 96.7\%, and Audit@10 of 99.5\%, 100.0\% and 100.0\%, respectively. Two prospective wet-lab syntheses demonstrate that ReTRACE proposals translate into executable procedures after expert revision.

papers.title: HiPPO Functional Memory: Coordinate-Queryable Attention for Irregular Time Series
papers.abstract: Irregular time series require models to answer temporal queries at arbitrary coordinates, yet existing approaches typically retain observation-dependent representations that must be repeatedly resolved for each query. We introduce HiPPO Functional Memory (HiPPO-FM), a functional-memory attention operator that compiles an irregular history into a reusable coordinate-addressable state. Instead of storing observation-indexed tokens or latent trajectories, HiPPO-FM writes observations into a fixed-rank functional space and performs direct coordinate evaluation through matched functional geometry. Kernel-smoothed HiPPO coordinates and Gram-based readout define a shared write/read mechanism, while observed-support self-attention enables content-dependent representations before compression. We characterize the induced finite-dimensional query space and derive an error decomposition separating functional geometry approximation from learned-memory mismatch. Across continuous-coordinate reconstruction, irregular representation learning, real-world extrapolation, and event-sequence prediction, HiPPO-FM consistently improves strong irregular time-series baselines, achieving strong reconstruction accuracy on Spiral, competitive performance across 20 UEA datasets, improved real-world extrapolation, and superior results on several irregular event benchmarks. After encoding, the compact functional state can be reused across different query sets without reprocessing the observation history.

papers.title: FlashReFocus: Interactive Image Refocusing in Seconds
papers.abstract: Single-image refocusing changes the focal plane and depth of field of a photograph after capture. Users compare focal choices on one photograph, so content stability across edits matters alongside quality and speed. Recent generative methods rerun large diffusion models for every edit, even when they first restore an all-in-focus image, so content can change inconsistently between edits. Yet only this restoration is highly ill-posed and benefits from a generative prior, whereas rendering blur is largely determined by depth and the focal plane. We therefore propose FlashReFocus, which runs diffusion once per photograph and renders each edit with a lightweight network. A one-step diffusion deblurrer with a decoder refiner recovers fine detail efficiently while balancing fidelity and perceptual quality. The renderer uses an explicit defocus map for control and defocus-bias attention to promote information exchange between tokens with similar blur magnitudes. Because every edit reuses the same reconstruction, in-focus content stays consistent across edits, and editing the map enables tilt-shift and two-plane effects. We further collect 3CReal, a benchmark of 89 pairs from three camera-lens systems, to evaluate generalization to unseen optics. For zero-shot bokeh rendering on EBB! Val176 and 3CReal, FlashReFocus leads the evaluated methods in fidelity and perceptual quality. At 1536x1536, a complete refocus takes 2.45 s and each subsequent edit 0.46 s on one RTX PRO 6000.

papers.title: UniField++: A Unified Agentic Framework with Loop Reasoning for MRI Field-Strength Enhancement
papers.abstract: Magnetic resonance imaging (MRI) field-strength enhancement seeks to combine the accessibility of low-field scanners with the image quality of high-field scanners. Yet, existing methods remain prone to anatomical hallucinations: scarce paired data limit knowledge of field-strength-dependent tissue contrast and anatomical visibility, while uniform processing leaves difficult brain regions with insufficient reasoning and refinement. To address these challenges by better coupling field-aware learning with region-adaptive reasoning and refinement, we propose UniField++, a two-agent framework for unified multi-field enhancement, including 64mT-to-3T and 3T-to-7T. Unified learning exposes both the vision-language model (VLM)-based planner and the flow-matching-based enhancer to field-dependent image characteristics across tasks. Trained with radiologists' annotations of field-dependent hallucination-prone brain regions and corresponding tissue- and anatomy-specific correction plans, the planner predicts regional risk and formulates targeted restoration strategies. Guided by these plans, the enhancer performs loop reasoning along the flow-matching trajectory, repeatedly processing high-risk brain regions for additional reasoning and refinement. Together, multi-field unification and risk-guided reasoning support anatomically faithful enhancement across field strengths. Across the evaluated tasks, UniField++ improves PSNR by an average of 2.74 dB and SSIM by 14.05 percentage points over comparison methods, with corresponding gains of 3.97 dB and 13.92 percentage points over the ablation baseline. It also maintains enhancement quality on an external cohort with an unseen field strength and improves downstream whole-brain segmentation Macro Dice by 0.1457 on average over original low-field inputs. Code: https://github.com/CUHK-AIM-Group/UniField_plusplus.

papers.title: Optimized linear multistep methods for stiff problems
papers.abstract: We design and test optimized linear multistep methods for stiff problems. Each method is A-stable, implicit, and second-order accurate. We focus on achieving the smallest possible error constant while also ensuring that stiff modes are damped. We recover some known optimal L-stable three- and four-step methods and prove their global optimality, and provide a new five-step method with essentially optimal error constant. We also study methods that are not L-stable but provide a prescribed rate of damping in the infinitely stiff limit; in particular, we prove that a known two-step family is optimal. Variable-step-size formulae are also provided for the L-stable methods. Numerical tests demonstrate that the improved error constants lead to improved accuracy.

papers.title: The Ephemeral Cost of Switching Optimizers Across LLM Training Stages
papers.abstract: Recent work suggests that switching optimizers between pretraining and subsequent training stages incurs a performance cost, but systematic investigation of this phenomenon is lacking. We study the mismatch between AdamW and Muon optimizers by pretraining 1.2B Llama-3 models from scratch while varying the proportion of updates taken with each optimizer, and similarly interpolating between the two optimizers during continued pretraining and supervised fine-tuning (SFT). Surprisingly, we find little evidence of a meaningful optimizer mismatch penalty: final performance is largely explained by the independent effects of the pretraining and post-training optimizers, with downstream performance generally improving as the proportion of Muon updates during SFT increases. Although matching the pretraining optimizer can reduce forgetting during SFT, this does not translate into improved final benchmark performance. We further evaluate AdamW and Muon for task-general SFT of open-weight models, across the Llama and Qwen families up to 14B parameters, where Muon remains competitive with AdamW, despite these models having been pretrained with AdamW. Finally, we investigate whether our findings extend to RL via experiments on our 1.2B models as well as Qwen3-1.7B and 4B, and find that AdamW and Muon achieve comparable final performance in math RLVR. Together, our results suggest that the choice of optimizer for post-training can be made largely independently of the optimizer used during pretraining.

papers.title: Post-merger rotational evolution of magnetised single hot subdwarfs results in slow rotation due to magnetic braking
papers.abstract: Single hot subdwarfs are believed to form through mergers of helium-core white dwarfs, which can lead to large-scale magnetic fields generated during the merger, and may be observable at the surface once they evolve into the stable core-helium burning phase. As a post-merger product, the orbital angular momentum of the binary system that forms it, could lead to a rapidly rotating hot subdwarf. But previous models were not able to explain the rather slow rotational velocities of observed single hot subdwarfs. Motivated by recent detections of surface magnetic fields in hot subdwarfs in the range 200 - 500 kiloGauss, we explore in this work the role of large-scale magnetic fields on their rotational evolution via rotating stellar evolution models. We find that large-scale stable magnetic fields can extract angular momentum efficiently from the star via coupling to stellar winds, producing slowly rotating single hot subdwarfs and thus providing a possible explanation to both the long rotation periods provided by asteroseismology and low spectroscopic rotational velocities. This hints magnetic braking could be an important component of the rotational properties of low-mass stellar mergers.

papers.title: BridgeTwist: Twisting Schrödinger Bridges for Training-Free Conditional Sampling
papers.abstract: Generative models are often required to serve many downstream conditional tasks. In the training-free setting, a pretrained unconditional model is reused as a prior and combined with a task-specific likelihood to sample from the corresponding posterior. While such training-free samplers have been developed for diffusion and flow models, their counterpart for Schrödinger bridge (SB) models remains unexplored, despite the growing appeal of SBs as flexible stochastic transport models between general source and target distributions. We propose BridgeTwist, a training-free conditional sampler for pretrained SB generative models, formulated as a tempered twisted sequential Monte Carlo scheme. The twist function employs a plug-in surrogate built on a closed-form endpoint predictor, which is derived by combining the velocity and score fields obtained from the SB pretraining. Since this surrogate is less reliable near the source, we temper the twist function with a time-varying exponent, downweighting its influence at early steps. We further introduce a bridge-shaped inference-time diffusion schedule that concentrates the proposal noise in the interior of the path. Telescoping importance weights then cancel all intermediate twist factors, yielding an asymptotically exact sampler for the posterior. Empirically, BridgeTwist outperforms training-free baselines on class-conditional and text-prompted image generation, and is competitive with specialized inverse problem solvers on inpainting, deblurring, and super-resolution.

papers.title: Urbex: Agentic Spatial Grounding for City-Scale 3D Scenes
papers.abstract: City-scale 3D grounding is commonly formulated as candidate ranking, which requires precomputed instance proposals and becomes inefficient in large outdoor scenes. We propose Urbex, an agentic vision-language framework that instead casts grounding as active spatial search. Urbex represents a city-scale 3D scene as an interactive multi-view environment, allowing a VLM agent to query landmarks, zoom into local regions, render oblique views, and commit a grounded bounding box. We optimize this tool-use policy with reinforcement learning on CityRefer, using smooth localization rewards and lightweight shaping rewards for efficient exploration. Experiments show that Urbex achieves the best Hit@1 and IoU on CityRefer, supports candidate-free grounding without ground-truth boxes, and is substantially faster than the strongest city-scale ranking baseline. Zero-shot results on STPLS3D-Refer further indicate improved cross-scene robustness.

papers.title: The interpreter as developer: An autoethnographic design study of building a computer-assisted interpreting tool through human-LLM co-creation
papers.abstract: Computer-assisted interpreting (CAI) tools are built for interpreters, mainly by third parties, and the interpreters' own side of development has received little first-person documentation. This article reports an autoethnographic design study in which a professional conference interpreter without formal programming training built a local-first CAI system through expert-led human-LLM co-creation. Analysis of the development dialogues shows how tacit professional knowledge became design only after generic defaults had failed in use, a reversal of the usual direction of technological mediation, from adopting tools to authoring them. Three mechanisms of in-booth appropriation emerged under a human-led division of labor, and a four-layer reconstruction illustrates the human contribution at work. First-month telemetry, over six thousand utterances across nine sessions, shows a fully local system sustaining translation-stage latencies near one second, with sustained-load degradation as a working boundary. The case bears on professional agency, knowledge production, and the training of interpreters under generative AI.

papers.title: Wyner's Common Information and the Common Entropy are NP-Hard to Compute
papers.abstract: Wyner's common information $J(P_{XY})$ and the common entropy $G(P_{XY})$ of a pair of finite random variables $(X,Y)$ with joint distribution $P_{XY}$ minimize, respectively, the mutual information $I(X,Y;W)$ and the entropy $H(W)$ over all auxiliary random variables $W$ that make $X$ and $Y$ conditionally independent. We prove that both quantities are NP-hard to compute, by polynomial-time reductions from the Maximum Edge Biclique problem. Moreover, unless $\mathrm{P}=\mathrm{NP}$, no polynomial-time algorithm can approximate $J(P_{XY})$ within an additive error $1/(8N^2)$, or $G(P_{XY})$ within an additive error $1/(2N)$, where $N$ is the number of positive entries of $P_{XY}$.

papers.title: confoundvis: an R package for sensitivity analysis of risk differences and established robustness measures for unmeasured confounding
papers.abstract: Observational studies of binary outcomes often lead to practical decisions. For example, does a treatment add a meaningful number of deaths per 100 patients? Sensitivity analysis asks how strong an unmeasured confounder would have to be to change such a conclusion. Bringing an estimate down to a practically important size and bringing it to zero are different questions, and they can need very different confounders. We present the R package confoundvis, which stores any one-dimensional sensitivity analysis in a common object and applies the same plotting, reporting, and tabulation functions to it. Version 0.4.1 adds sens_risk_difference(), which applies the binary-confounder model of Lin, Psaty, and Kronmal to a fitted model. This function standardizes the risks to the study population and reports where the risk difference reaches a user-chosen threshold and where it reaches zero. The package also computes the omitted-variable-bias bounds of the Python package doubleml for fits from the R package DoubleML, imports instrumental-variable sensitivity analyses from iv.sensemakr, and runs partial R2, impact-threshold, replacement, E-value, and Rosenbaum analyses through one call. In the right heart catheterization data (5,735 patients), catheterization was associated with 6.3 more deaths within 30 days per 100 patients (95% CI 3.7 to 8.9). For a confounder present in 40% of catheterized and 20% of other patients, an odds ratio of 3.39 with death brought the difference down to an illustrative threshold of 2 deaths per 100. On the other hand, an odds ratio of 6.37 was needed to bring it to zero. All results agreed with the established implementations.

papers.title: Levy-shaped femtoscopic sources from an exact solution of relativistic hydrodynamics
papers.abstract: An important goal of high-energy physics is to better understand the spacetime structure of particle emitting sources created in heavy-ion collisions. For a fraction of a second, a special form of matter, the so-called quark-gluon plasma (QGP), is created, which can be examined with the toolkit of femtoscopy. With the measurement of correlation functions it was determined that Lévy distributions describe the shape of hadron (pion) emission sources at freeze-out the most accurately; however, analytic solutions of hydrodynamics typically yield Gaussian sources, and power-law tails are usually attributed to the hadronic stage rather than to the fluid dynamics itself. In this article we showcase an exact solution of the equations of relativistic hydrodynamics, which aims to resolve this puzzle by providing Lévy distributions directly from hydrodynamics. A detailed analysis reveals whether the predictions of this solution are in accordance with observations; in particular, the effective temperatures from angle-averaged transverse mass distributions and the femtoscopic radii from two-particle momentum correlation functions are analyzed.

papers.title: An explicit tame factorization of the four-variable Anick automorphism
papers.abstract: Let $δ=xz-yt$. We give an explicit tame factorization of the Anick automorphism $$ f=(x+δt,y+δz,z,t) $$ of $F[x,y,z,t]$. After a linear change of coordinates, the factorization consists of sixteen elementary automorphisms, all fixing $z$. The proof uses a commutator construction with variables already present in the algebra. A complete list of the elementary factors is included in Section 5. The explicit polynomial factorization identities are defined over $Z[1/2]$; no conclusion in characteristic $2$ is asserted. We also prove that the Freudenburg--Moser-Jauslin involution $$ τ(a,b,x,y)= \bigl(b,a,-b^3x+(1+ab+a^2b^2)y,(1-ab)x+a^3y\bigr). $$ of $F[a,b,x,y]$ is tame over every field of characteristic different from $2$ and $3$, and list an explicit factorization in Appendix.

papers.title: YUBI-STAG: Contact and Semantic-Rich Alignment for VLAs via Automated Video-Language Grounding
papers.abstract: Vision-Language-Action (VLA) models acquire broad manipulation capabilities via large-scale pretraining, yet eliciting them through language requires fine-grained alignment between instructions and physical interactions. Existing robot demonstrations typically provide only coarse task descriptions, omitting how actions are executed, including which gripper acts, which object is contacted, and how it is grasped and moved. We introduce YUBI-STAG, a framework for Spatio-Temporal Annotation and Grounding that automatically enriches manipulation demonstrations with interaction-rich semantics to align pretrained VLAs with fine-grained manipulation language. Combining contact-object segmentation with vision-language models, YUBI-STAG annotates object identities, attributes and states, per-gripper actions, bimanual coordination, and spatially grounded interactions. To address YUBI-STAG's reliance on localized sequences and multi-stage VLM inference, we distill it into YUBI-VLM. YUBI-VLM directly recovers action structure and annotations from raw, unsegmented video in few inference calls and operates from wrist views alone. We evaluate both frameworks on YUBI-STAG-Bench across temporal, semantic, and spatial grounding tasks. YUBI-VLM retains much of YUBI-STAG's annotation accuracy with fewer inference calls and shorter runtime while generalizing to unseen manipulations. Finally, post-training VLA policies on these annotations aligns them with fine-grained language and contact-aware structure. Bimanual experiments demonstrate improved performance and instruction following, including control over object identity, acting gripper, target location, and spatial relations absent from original labels.

papers.title: RoboPace: Contact-Aware Time-Optimal Retiming for Action-Chunk Policies
papers.abstract: Robot manipulation data collection has been shifting from teleoperation toward robot-free demonstrations, through interfaces such as the Universal Manipulation Interface (UMI) or directly from human hands. Vision-Language-Action (VLA) policies trained on such data inherit the demonstrator's timing. Yet human timing does not directly transfer to robots: compliant hands tolerate fast contact, whereas robots may overshoot due to actuator and tracking limitations; conversely, robots can move faster in free space. This motivates a unified approach that reconciles execution speed with contact safety. We present RoboPace, an online retiming layer that preserves the policy's geometric path while adapting its timing, respecting the target robot's kinematic and dynamic constraints. It adapts execution speed based on predicted contact, jointly accounting for contact-dependent speed limits and the robot's motion constraints. The method requires no policy retraining and operates in real time. Across three contact-rich tasks on a dual-arm robot, faster uniform execution and physical-limit-only retiming largely fail. RoboPace instead achieves higher overall success than slow uniform execution while completing four of five commands in approximately half the time, retaining the reliability of slow execution without its time cost.

papers.title: Targeted Modality Dropout for Real-Robot Manipulation Robust to Intermittent Vision Loss
papers.abstract: Imitation learning policies that integrate multiple sensory modalities are prone to overreliance on a dominant modality, such as vision, during training, which can disrupt policy execution when that modality is lost at inference time. In this paper, we introduce Targeted Modality Dropout (TMD), in which the dependence on each modality is estimated using attention and the most dominant modality is selectively dropped during training. This is combined with entropy regularization over the dependence distribution. We evaluate six tasks on a real bimanual manipulator, simulating intermittent vision loss by jointly masking all vision tokens with 10% probability per inference chunk. Baseline successes decrease from 14/30 under normal conditions to 2/30 under vision loss, whereas TMD maintains an aggregate count of 15/30. TMD also exhibits smaller changes in action commands when chunks generated under vision loss arrive. In contrast, a conventional dropout that selects the dropped modality at random, without the entropy regularization, fails on many tasks even without vision loss.

papers.title: Plunge bounds for Fourier concentration operators: geometry, smoothing, and wave packets
papers.abstract: We prove a single-logarithm bound for the eigenvalues in the plunge region of Fourier concentration operators, removing the extra logarithmic factor in the Kulikov--Dam Larsen bound for two general admissible sets throughout each fixed exponential window. For bounded spatial and frequency sets $A,B\subset\mathbb{R}^d$ of positive measure with finite upper codimension-one Minkowski boundary content, the number $Λ_\varepsilon(cA,B)$ of eigenvalues in $(\varepsilon,1-\varepsilon)$ satisfies $Λ_\varepsilon(cA,B)\le C(d,A,B,β)c^{d-1}D(1+\log_+(c/D))$, where $D=\log(1/(\varepsilon(1-\varepsilon)))$, for every fixed $β>0$, $c\ge2$, $0<\varepsilon<1/2$, and $D\leβc$, with $\log_+t=\max(0,\log t)$. The argument uses positive band-limited smoothing and requires no symmetry, convexity, or connectedness. In dimension two, the corresponding exponential-window estimate has a constant uniform in the window parameter. We also determine the optimal coordinate-Lipschitz constant $d-1$ for recursive decompositions of balls and standard simplices in every dimension, and obtain box-frequency estimates with explicit geometric constants. For $C^1$ convex bodies in three dimensions, the optimal infimum of recursive coordinate slopes is $2$. Uniform real-order Bessel estimates give independent disk and ball bounds at every spectral threshold, including an explicit deep-tail term. For smooth strictly convex planar frequency bodies with positive curvature, we prove correlation estimates for aligned Gaussian packets at arbitrary relative scales and quantitative lower bounds on the cost of estimating spatial blocks separately. Together these results connect the global spectral bound with sharp geometric constructions and the cancellation retained by grouping boundary interactions.

papers.title: Armillary: A Label-Free Coordinate System for Stellar Spectra
papers.abstract: A stellar spectrum is determined by a few parameters, so a set of spectra lies on a low-dimensional manifold with those parameters as its coordinates. We introduce Armillary, which generalises the Sequencer of Baron and Ménard from an ordering to multidimensional coordinates, constructed from the spectra alone. Two stars are compared by the Wasserstein distance between their signed absorption profiles. Shortest paths through a nearest-neighbour graph measure distance along the manifold and give the coordinates, and the same graph transfers the labels of a few stars to all the others. The coordinates are more nearly linear in $T_{\rm eff}$ and $\log g$ than principal components, t-SNE, UMAP or an autoencoder. The label transfer, without deep learning, is more precise than the first three and comparable to the autoencoder. On 202,932 APOGEE DR17 stars, an illustrative draw of 32 training stars recovers the ASPCAP $T_{\rm eff}$, $\log g$ and [M/H] of held-out dwarfs and giants, with $1σ$ errors of 100 K, 0.18 and 0.083 dex. Resolving the two $α$ sequences of the disc in [$α$/M] for giants takes 128 training stars, and with 2048 the four errors improve to 33 K, 0.06, 0.026 and 0.022 dex. On 104,799 DESI stars, 32 training labels from APOGEE recover the stellar parameters to 129 K, 0.25 and 0.203 dex, even for spectra degraded to a signal-to-noise of about 20. At a signal-to-noise of about 100, 2048 labels resolve the two $α$ sequences of the disc in DESI giants, with errors against APOGEE of 51 K, 0.07, 0.047 and 0.026 dex. The code and the data products are at https://github.com/tingyuansen/armillary.

papers.title: Black Hole Entropy and Holographic Entanglement Entropy in DGP Brane Gravity
papers.abstract: We investigate the relation between gravitational entropy and holographic entanglement entropy in braneworld gravity with gravitational dynamics localized on the brane. We first consider the DGP brane model, in which an Einstein-Hilbert term is included in the brane action, and demonstrate that the gravitational entropy of a braneworld black hole agrees with the holographic entanglement entropy for general stationary spacetimes. We then generalize the brane-localized Einstein-Hilbert term to higher-curvature gravitational theories. For Lovelock gravity and $f(R)$ gravity on the brane, we derive the corresponding expressions for gravitational entropy and holographic entanglement entropy and show that the two entropies also coincide for general stationary spacetimes. These results establish the equivalence between gravitational entropy and holographic entanglement entropy in braneworld gravity for a broad class of gravitational theories and contribute to a deeper understanding of holography in braneworld settings.

papers.title: Recovering Parallelism under Fixed Numerical References in Quantized LLM Decoders
papers.abstract: Splitting a quantized decoder at a physical attention-view boundary can break projection groups that already match a fixed numerical reference. LOCAL retains those groups, partitions queries by physical view inside attention, and rejoins the outputs in query order. Owned score rows survive native-buffer reuse, and commit supplies the key-value (KV) and consumer state for the next call. At a fixed 32B attention-view crossing on A5000 with frozen proposals, LOCAL reduces verification-through-commit time by 21.56% against SIMPLE (the whole-call splitting baseline). This supporting endpoint covers 12 paired time blocks (95% CI [20.21%, 22.83%]). In the primary noncrossing history, both arms retain the four-column projection and the estimated reduction is 0.43% [-1.13%, 2.01%]. This comparison measures the two implementations when neither fragments the projection group. Across two fixed 8B conversations under target-only decoding, the primary equal-weight estimate was a 1.44% reduction in response-plus-reset time (95% CI [-0.82%, 3.85%]). Separate studies with SIMPLE fixed report request-time reductions from few-column execution (C4) and packing of admitted groups (P4); the RTX C4 contrasts are descriptive secondary results. The fixed-crossing result demonstrates that attention can observe its physical-view boundaries while projection retains parallel work under the same numerical reference.

papers.title: Study of the Ultra-Long GRB 220627A: Exploring a Possible Blue Supergiant Collapsar Origin
papers.abstract: Ultra-long gamma-ray bursts (ul-GRBs) challenge standard collapsar models because their extreme durations require central engines active for $\sim10^{3}-10^{4}$ s. While the prompt spectral evolution of typical GRBs is difficult to resolve due to their short durations, ul-GRBs provide a unique opportunity to study spectral evolution on extended timescales. We present a time-resolved spectroscopic study of GRB 220627A, one of the most luminous ul-GRBs known ($E_{\rm iso}\sim10^{54}$ erg, $T_{90}>1000$ s), consisting of two bright emission episodes separated by $\sim600$ s quiescent interval. Using a novel HOP algorithm-based segmentation method, we identify optimal time intervals for time-resolved spectroscopy. A Comptonized power-law (CPL) model well describes the prompt emission ($\sim 10$ keV-40 MeV) across all timescales. Fermi-GBM spectroscopy reveals a transition from a hard, slow-cooling synchrotron spectrum ($α_{\rm I}=-0.70$) during episode-I to a softer, fast-cooling synchrotron spectrum ($α_{\rm II}=-1.29$) during episode-II. This evolution closely resembles that of the magnetar-candidate GRB 091024A, highlighting a potential progenitor degeneracy based solely on spectral evolution. However, the extreme isotropic-equivalent energy exceeds the maximum energy available from magnetar spin-down, strongly favouring a blue supergiant (BSG) collapsar origin. The prolonged activity and multi-episode structure are naturally explained by sustained accretion through an extended stellar envelope. Our results demonstrate that ul-GRBs can display magnetar-like spectral evolution while being powered by BSG collapsars. GRB 220627A highlights the need for combining time-resolved spectroscopy with energetic constraints to distinguish between progenitor scenarios and understand the physical origin of ul-GRBs.

papers.title: Made to Measure: Designing Image Watermarks to Specification
papers.abstract: Image watermarking enables provenance and attribution, but practical deployments must jointly satisfy robustness, false-positive rate (FPR), image quality, and latency requirements. Existing watermarking methods offer complementary robustness against different attacks, making their composition attractive for broader protection. However, combining watermarks introduces interference, distortion, decoding overhead, and additional verification paths that share the same FPR budget. We propose TAILOR, a request-conditioned watermark composition framework with three stages: (1) offline characterization models fragment recovery, distortion, latency, and composition interactions across embedding strengths; (2) joint configuration selection uses satisfiability modulo theories (SMT) to jointly optimize fragment selection, continuous embedding strengths, embedding order, and geometric recovery while minimizing predicted distortion; and (3) live calibration validates candidate configurations on user images and refines inaccurate offline predictions to improve deployment success. Across 7,321 distinct deployment requests spanning five scenarios and 20 attack settings, TAILOR achieves 96.21% scenario-averaged request satisfaction with a mean PSNR of 41.02 dB, demonstrating its effectiveness in meeting diverse deployment requirements while maintaining high image fidelity. Code is available at https://github.com/aaFrostnova/Tailor.

papers.title: A Pogorelov-type estimate for the real twisted Monge-Ampère equation
papers.abstract: We establish a Pogorelov type interior $C^2$ estimate for the real twisted Monge-Ampere equation without assuming uniform ellipticity. This equation is fully nonlinear and elliptic, but is neither concave nor a function of the eigenvalues of the Hessian, so the standard techniques for interior second-derivative estimates do not directly apply. Building on the partial Legendre transform formulation of Streets and Warren, we derive a differential identity for the associated positive-definite matrix $W(D^2u)$ and use some linear algebra to control the third-order terms arising in the maximum principle argument. As an application, we prove a Liouville theorem for entire split convex solutions with quadratic growth, extending the rigidity theorem of Streets and Warren by replacing their uniform ellipticity hypothesis with suitable quadratic growth assumptions.

papers.title: Transcending Algebraic Geometry
papers.abstract: We give an exposition of some of the ideas leading up to Jacob Tsimerman's groundbreaking work developing the theory of o-minimal definability in arithmetic and algebraic geometry.

papers.title: A question of Ulam and a theorem of de Rham
papers.abstract: We generalize de Rham's decomposition theorem to proper metric spaces: every proper metric space has a unique decomposition as the product of a Euclidean space and a finite or countable pointed $\ell^2$-product of nontrivial irreducible non-Euclidean factors. A slightly weaker unique decomposition statement is verified for general complete metric spaces. We use this to resolve a question of Ulam on the uniqueness of square roots of complete metric spaces.

papers.title: More RLBWT Tricks
papers.abstract: Indexes based on $k$-mers can beat BWT-based indexes when the former take advantage of unitigs in de Bruijn graphs. In this paper we consider ways in which BWT-based indexes can do that as well, or even better. In particular, we consider MEM-finding between human chromosome 19s, where we can achieve a five- to sevenfold speedup over plain backward search, or a two- to threefold speedup over plain backward search with latency hiding, for about twice the space.

papers.title: Non-Hermitian Yang--Mills Connections with Vanishing Chern Classes
papers.abstract: We construct non-flat non-Hermitian Yang--Mills connections with vanishing Chern classes whose induced and conjugate-dual holomorphic bundles are both stable, giving a negative answer to Kaledin and Verbitsky's flatness question even under these stability assumptions. We also give negative answers to their questions about the étaleness and bijectivity of the harmonic-class map. The examples are explicit connections on smoothly trivial rank-two bundles over projective Kähler surfaces and admit explicit positive harmonic metrics. For the family of fixed stable bundles studied here, the harmonic-class map is surjective. Every fibre contains exactly one flat point, but some fibres also contain positive-dimensional families of non-flat connections. The entire flat locus is a smooth component mapped biholomorphically onto the target. For a range of parameters, we determine the complete reduced analytic germ at a distinguished nonunitary flat point. It has two smooth branches of different dimensions whose intersection contains two-sided stable points arbitrarily close to that point. Finally, a single fibre of the pair of holomorphic projections contains infinitely many flat classes and an embedded copy of $\CC^*$ with exactly two flat members. Thus the two holomorphic isomorphism classes together do not determine flatness.

papers.title: Beyond Accuracy: Prefix-Invariant Realizations of Low-Precision Fast Matrix Multiplication
papers.abstract: Fast matrix multiplication saves multiplications through exact cancellation, but rounding sums that mix token rows can leave contributions from later tokens in earlier language model outputs. This threatens prefix invariance, which likelihood scoring and batched inference rely on: an output must depend only on its allowed prefix. On Qwen2.5-14B-Instruct, two fast FP8 realizations repaired to near-bf16 accuracy, and the existing fast kernel FalconGEMM, change answers when only text outside the allowed prefix is replaced: on 4.17--10.00% of OpenBookQA items scored by likelihood and 39.6--51.8% of NQ-open questions answered in a batch. Accuracy thus does not certify prefix invariance, and the stability criteria we analyze cannot tell realizations apart: across all 512 sign variants of two-level Strassen the criteria stay constant while teacher-forced perplexities span a 772.4$\times$ range on the same model. We therefore construct certified realizations of two-level Strassen on bounded integer codes that quantize token rows independently, then mix and cancel exactly before rescaling, using 49 block multiplications instead of 64. Our certificate guarantees bitwise equality to a prescribed row-local classical int8 operator at the same quantization specification, so every certified realization inherits its prefix invariance. Certification thus turns realization choice into a pure cost decision: which certified realization runs can no longer change any output. With optimized kernels, certified realizations run faster than classical int8 on an NVIDIA H20, and in the SGLang serving engine they raise throughput over its FP8 path by 1.2--5.6% on four models.

papers.title: Quantum-echo Markov process for combinatorial optimization
papers.abstract: We introduce a quantum-echo Markov process for combinatorial optimization. Quantum dynamics based on quantum annealing (QA) or the quantum approximate optimization algorithm (QAOA) is used to engineer the transition kernel. Increasing the annealing time in QA or the number of layers in QAOA enables transitions to explore distant configurations while suppressing large energy changes. The Hamming-space delocalization originates from operator spreading, whereas the energy-space localization arises from a dynamically generated correlation. For optimization, we propose quantum-echo local optimization. For the ferromagnetic Ising chain, increasing the annealing time or circuit depth yields a nearly quadratic improvement in the dependence of the mean first-passage time on the inverse optimality gap compared with random single-spin flips. For the random Ising model, increasing these parameters initially improves optimization performance, whereas further increases degrade performance in QA and lead to saturation in QAOA. Quantum-echo greedy descent substantially improves the performance, highlighting the complementary roles of quantum dynamics in exploration and greedy descent in exploitation. These results establish quantum-echo dynamics as a framework for engineering structured transition kernels and provide a route to using finite-resource quantum many-body dynamics as a computational primitive for iterative optimization.

papers.title: Exploring the Hidden Cost of the World Around AI Agents
papers.abstract: Agent benchmarks test what agents can do in environments that are built for their tasks. Deployed agents work in the real world where other people and tools can change the state. An agent booking a flight may receive a message from someone else to change the destination, or a booking tool may fail without saying whether the ticket was purchased. We present BACKDROP, which asks how much of an agent's capability in a clean world survives in a non-cooperative world. BACKDROP takes a task along with the agent's execution environment, and plants four everyday hazards in its environment, one at a time and all together. Each hazard tests a different behavior. Authority: does a non-author actor instruction, from anyone who did not author the task, override the user's goal? Injection: does text planted in a record redirect the agent? Boundary: does the agent make changes in an app the user's task did not require? Fault: after a write fails without saying whether it landed, does the agent check before it retries? Across 3,678 variants and 16 models, the average pass rate falls from 69.5% to 31.3% once all four hazards are present; the strongest models fall furthest (Claude Fable 5.1 from 96.6% to 56.0%). The gap is consistent throughout all 16 models. BACKDROP formalizes these gaps and shows how an agent's score in a task's world is a ceiling on real-world performance.

papers.title: Learning via Self-Consistency for Diffusion-based Video Reasoning
papers.abstract: While video diffusion models have demonstrated emerging zero-shot capability for visual reasoning and perception tasks, their stochastic generations often produce inconsistent predictions for tasks requiring reliable, structured outputs. Prior work has shown that self-consistency across stochastic video generations can improve diffusion-based reasoning at test time. We systematically extend the test-time method to structured prediction problems such as referring segmentation. However, test time scaling via self-consistency requires multiple rollouts and incurs much more latency. We propose self-consistency as an intrinsic learning signal for post-training video diffusion models without ground truth annotations or external verifiers. Specifically, our proposed Self-Consistency Fine-Tuning (SC-FT) distills consensus predictions into the video generation model, while subsequent Self-Consistency Reinforcement Learning (SC-RL) rewards generations according to their agreement with the consensus. The resulting model effectively internalizes the benefit of multi-sample consensus and requires only a single generation at inference time, while substantially outperforming the original model. To further reduce inference overhead, we read out predictions early in the denoising trajectory, preserving consensus quality while cutting inference time per rollout by 52%. For visual search, our method raises task accuracy from 48.4% for a single generation to 99.1%. For maze solving across three layout sizes, SC-FT and SC-RL improve single generation strict validity from 59.1% to 66.1% and 95.6% with the same inference latency. Also, for referring segmentation, SC-RL raises single-generation gIoU from 0.402 to 0.582, beyond SC-FT 0.473.

papers.title: Using the Whole Slice: AlphaFold2 Inference on an Eight-Chip TPU v5e
papers.abstract: AlphaFold2 is written in JAX. JAX treats each chip of a tensor processing unit (TPU) slice as a separate device. A JAX program does not spread its work over the chips by itself, so a user who runs AlphaFold2 on a slice can pay for chips that do nothing. We found no published measurement of how AlphaFold2 inference uses a multi-chip TPU slice. Our goal was to measure how much of an eight-chip TPU v5e slice AlphaFold2 inference uses, and which way of mapping the work in JAX uses all of it. Across 12 experiments, the model used random weights, so we studied execution, not prediction quality. By default, only one chip held data. Batching up to eight input sequences (queries) of 118 residues on one chip with JAX's vmap did not raise throughput. Mapping independent queries to the chips with JAX's pmap ran them in parallel on all eight chips. On a grid of 1 to 8 chips and 100 to 1000 residues, eight chips gave 6.5 to 7.9 times the throughput of one chip. JAX's automatic partitioning did not shorten the call for one query. Our program did not tell the partitioner how to split any array across the chips.

papers.title: Anomalous Hardening of a Fluctuation-Induced Gap
papers.abstract: In a mean-field picture, a gap opened by quantum fluctuations grows with them. This can fail if the fluctuating mode is critical and its displacement compensates its coupling to the degenerate states. A single parameter sets the gap response: above a universal threshold, the gap hardens as the critical fluctuations weaken. Whenever the parameter is nonzero, overcompensation beyond the critical point drives a secondary phase transition. In a quantum Rabi ring with synthetic flux, exact diagonalization shows the gap of a photonic Landau level rising by 15% as the critical variance falls by 25%.

papers.title: An adaptive $L_2$-type test for high-dimensional white noise
papers.abstract: We propose a new $L_2$-type test for white noise which allows the dimension $p$ of the time series to either (i) be a fixed constant, or (ii) diverge with the sample size $n$. The proposed test statistic exhibits an interesting phase transition, following two different regimes of behavior: $p$ is fixed, and $p\rightarrow\infty$. Because identification of the operable regime is difficult, if not impossible in practice, we devise a novel adaptive bootstrap method to construct a unified testing procedure across different phases. Numerical experiments confirm the good finite sample performance of the proposed adaptive $L_2$-type test in comparison to the existing methods in the literature. The proposed testing procedure has been implemented in R package HDTSA.

papers.title: Resolving State-Representation Mismatch: State-Space Visual Reasoning for Open-Loop VLA Planning
